My early-2015 Macbook Pro came with a 500GB solid state drive. Solid state drives are great. You can store more data per unit of volume, they retrieve data faster, and since there are no moving parts they are less susceptible to wear and tear.

But they are more expensive per unit of storage. At the time I bought the laptop, laptop hard disk drives were in the terabyte range.

Inevitably, my drive filled up. Once it got down below 10 GB, some regular behind-the-scenes processes ran the chance of filling up the drive completely. I offloaded a lot of large files (mostly scans of quizzes and exams) to my Box account, wihch has unlimited storage through my university's license. That freed up about 100GB. But it seemed like this was a process that was only going to get worse, so I looked into upgrading the drive.

# Hardware

Other World Computing has a nice "Upgrade my Mac" page that allows you to choose your model, and tells you what's available. They sell a 1TB solid state drive for about \$600. And they ship it with a kit that includes an enclosure for the drive, a cable to attach it to your computer, and two screwdrivers. One is the pentalobe screwdrive needed to open the Macbook's bottom cover, and the other is the Torx screwdriver needed to attach the drive to the computer's chassis.

Once these things arrived in the mail, I thought carefully about how I wanted to proceed.

OWC's recommended process is to:

> 1.  Remove the old drive from the computer and swap in the new, blank drive.
> 2.  Install the old drive in the enclosure, and attach it to the computer with the cable. So now you have an internal blank drive, and the former drive mounted externally.
> 3.  Boot the computer in recovery mode (with the ⌘R key combination once you see the Apple logo), and install MacOS on the blank drive.
> 4.  Use the Migration Assistant to copy user files and applications from the old drive (now mounted externally) to the new (internal) drive.

# First attempt: Carbon Copy Cloner

I wanted to avoid all the downtime required to install MacOS on a blank drive, then migrate several hundred gigabytes of data from the old drive to the new. The advice I was given at work was to:

> 1.  Install the new drive in the enclosure and mount it externally.
> 2.  Clone the original drive, still installed internally, to the new drive.
> 3.  Swap the drives, installing the new drive in place of the old one.
> 4.  Boot.

It seemed like this would work. The effect would be the exact same data on a larger drive.

I wondered how long it would take to complete the copying. Having done it before, I would have alotted at least eight hours to migrate a hard drive. Solid state drives are faster, but how much? According to one site, USB 3.1 allows for 5 gigabits transfer per second, which would mean 5 gigabytes in eight seconds, and 500 gigabytes in 800 seconds. 800 seconds is 13 minutes and 20 seconds. That seemed a little optimistic.
